newsitem.title: USA: Cell phone health study needs 5 yrs-U.S. officials.
newsitem.headline: Cell phone health study needs 5 yrs-U.S. officials.

text.p: Scientists will need at least five years to get a definitive answer about cancer risk or other possible health problems from low-level radiation emitted by millions of cellular phones and other wireless devices, U.S. health officials said Wednesday.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration officials told an advisory panel that they do not plan to seek more regulation pending the outcome of studies by the World Health Organization, the cellphone industry and other researchers.

Cell phones are not medical devices and are regulated primarily by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which last year started requiring manufacturers to start meeting a standard for radiation collected in brain tissue.
The FDA also has some regulatory authority, particularly over the radiation component.

There are at least 40 million cell phones used in the United States alone and FDA officials said there is some evidence from animal studies that cellphones can cause tumors or damage to genetic material.

It has not been firmly established the phones can cause brain tumors or other cancers in humans and health experts are seeking studies that would measure the effects of chronic exposure on human beings.

The Cellular Telecommunications Industry Association said they have pledged $25 million to study potential problems. Industry-sponsored research to date has not found any cancers in humans caused by these devices.

With the proliferation of wireless technology, the FDA expects to see more short and long term health effects, Don Witters of the FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH) said. It is also concerned the devices could interfere with electronic medical equipment, such as defibrillators, electric wheelchairs and ventilators.
A joint cell phone-pacemaker industry study led to a 1996 recommendation that phones in use be kept at least six inches away from the chest area in people with pacemakers.

Witters said the interference issue is likely to grow with the advent of digital phones, which pulse in a manner similar to the body's own electrophysiologic system. The phones also use a higher frequency -- closer to microwave ovens -- which may lead to more interruptions.
